query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introduction of grain boundary segregants or precipitates can improve the room-temperature ductility of Equal-atomic NbMoTaW without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but poor room-temperature ductility
generation.intervention: Controlled introduction of grain boundary segregants or precipitates

generation.mechanism: Grain boundary segregation or precipitation reduces grain boundary energy and promotes dislocation mobility, enhancing room-temperature ductility
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved room-temperature ductility by 20% relative to the untreated baseline, maintained mechanical performance at 1600 °C, and maintained irradiation resistance
generation.boundary: Composition: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW, Processing: Controlled introduction of grain boundary segregants or precipitates
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of improvement in room-temperature ductility and the optimal processing conditions for introducing grain boundary segregants or precipitates are uncertain
